[CONFLICT] The claim that GDP growth fails to capture non-material dimensions of wellbeing is disputed because while GDP measures economic output, it does not directly account for subjective factors like mental health or social cohesion, leading to disagreement over whether this omission constitutes a fundamental flaw or a limitation within its intended scope.

C004.subject: GDP per capita
C004.object: material living standards in developed economies with high public service provision
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies with high public service provision]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and national accounts data on in-kind public services (e.g., health, education) adjusted for household income — Directly tests whether GDP per capita diverges from alternative welfare measures that impute the value of public services, quantifying the underestimation in high-provision OECD economies.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative studies of household consumption and income distribution (e.g., Luxembourg Income Study) that include public service transfers — Provides micro-level evidence on how public service provision lifts material living standards beyond what GDP per capita captures, helping to confirm or refute the systematic bias.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical and empirical literature on 'GDP and welfare' (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission reports, Jones & Klenow 2016) — Synthesizes existing arguments and evidence on GDP's limitations as a welfare measure, offering a conceptual framework to assess the hypothesis and identify gaps in current data.

scope.domain: developed economies, material welfare, public goods

C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index data (2000-2020) comparing GDP per capita with composite material well-being indicators (e.g., housing, income, jobs) — Directly tests the correlation between GDP per capita and multidimensional material living standards across OECD countries post-2000, using official comparable data.

[PATH:literature] Piketty, T., & Saez, E. (2003). 'Income Inequality in the United States, 1913–1998.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, and subsequent updates to 2020 — Provides longitudinal evidence on how GDP growth diverges from median income and consumption trends, supporting the hypothesis that aggregate GDP per capita may not reflect material living standards for typical households in developed economies.

[PATH:theoretical] Stiglitz, J. E., Sen, A., & Fitoussi, J.-P. (2009). Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress — Offers a theoretical framework critiquing GDP per capita as a proxy for material welfare, proposing alternative metrics that can be used to empirically test the hypothesis.

C006.subject: GDP growth
C006.object: aggregate mental health indicators in developed economies over multi-decade periods
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth aggregate mental health indicators in developed economies over multi-decade periods]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of World Happiness Report data (1990-2020) combined with OECD GDP per capita growth rates, controlling for unemployment, inequality, and social spending — Directly tests the temporal and geographic scope of the hypothesis using repeated cross-sectional data on subjective wellbeing and economic output, allowing for fixed-effects models to isolate suppression effects over multi-decade periods.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies linking economic growth to mental health outcomes (e.g., depression, anxiety prevalence) in developed economies, e.g., from journals like Social Science & Medicine or The Lancet Public Health — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to assess whether the aggregate relationship is consistently negative, null, or positive, and identifies moderators such as income inequality or social safety nets that could explain the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from the 'Easterlin Paradox' literature and status competition models (e.g., Richard Easterlin, Robert Frank) applied to mental health trends — Provides causal mechanisms (e.g., relative income concerns, hedonic adaptation, work-life balance erosion) that would predict GDP growth suppressing mental health, offering testable predictions against the empirical data.

C007.subject: GDP growth
C007.object: improvements in non-material dimensions of wellbeing (e.g., mental health, social cohesion)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth improvements in non-material dimensions of wellbeing (e.g., mental health, social cohesion)]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and Gallup World Poll data (post-2000, OECD countries): correlate GDP growth rates with self-reported life satisfaction, mental health indices, and social support indicators. — Provides direct longitudinal, cross-national quantitative evidence on the relationship between economic growth and non-material wellbeing dimensions, allowing for panel regression or Granger causality tests.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox literature and meta-analyses (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010; Sacks, Stevenson & Wolfers, 2012) focusing on OECD countries after 2000. — Summarizes decades of debate on whether GDP growth yields lasting improvements in subjective wellbeing; a targeted update for post-2000 OECD data can clarify if the paradox holds or weakens in recent decades.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort studies (e.g., UK Understanding Society, German SOEP) tracking mental health and social cohesion alongside regional GDP changes. — Individual-level panel data can disentangle GDP growth effects from confounding factors (e.g., inequality, policy changes) and assess whether aggregate growth translates into non-material wellbeing improvements at the micro level.
